title: Networking 101 in 26 minutes from Harvard & Stanford MBAs
summary: A sister-only 'Networking 101 part two' episode with tactical advice on conferences and networking events, conversations with senior executives, and how to exit a conversation gracefully. Key takeaways: bring a buddy or make a conference buddy, read the room and use safe entry points like the bar or a first-timer opener, your own mindset and openness drive results, research attendees and speakers ahead of time, communicate with executives 'Twitter not Tolstoy' using a 15/5/2-minute exercise, build trust so you get the benefit of the doubt, and use a buddy or a thin polite excuse to leave a conversation.

ideas.idea: You don't have to go to a networking event alone; bring a buddy you can regroup, strategize and debrief with, or make it your goal to find a 'conference buddy' if you go solo.
ideas.detail: Cherie forwards every relevant conference to friends who would benefit. Jean adds that if you attend the same industry conferences you will see the same people, and someone who came alone will be relieved to pair up for future events.

ideas.idea: Networking events are one of the safest places to introduce yourself to strangers because everyone is there for a positive social experience; open with 'is this your first time at this event?'.
ideas.detail: Cherie contrasts it with the middle-school cafeteria feeling; the first-timer opener (e.g. 'is this your first VidCon?') works whether the answer is yes or 'I've been three or four times'.

ideas.idea: Read body language before approaching: never interrupt an intense one-on-one, but join large open circles, people standing alone, or someone getting food or a drink at the bar.
ideas.detail: Jean says two people locked in conversation are a 'see yourself out' zone; the bar or food area is a safe place to intercept someone and break the ice.

ideas.idea: How much you get out of a conference depends mostly on your own internal mindset, mood and openness going in, so hype yourself up, or give yourself grace and skip it if you truly can't.
ideas.detail: Jean flew to the Shoptalk conference in London as a Snapchat vendor after an exhausting week of onsites, was in a 'state of non-openness', could barely talk to people, and the conference was almost a total wash. Cherie once had to give a speech in Chinese at a Shanghai conference and had no energy left for networking; attending for work with vendor goals is very different from attending for yourself.

ideas.idea: There is serendipity in networking: each additional conversation raises the odds one is great, and one event tends to open doors to after-parties, lunches and future events.
ideas.detail: A friend who went to a conference alone after failing to recruit buddies shared an Uber with a conference organizer and got invited to another conference for free. Cherie's line: instead of 'what's the worst that can happen', ask 'what's the best that can happen?'.

ideas.idea: Skip the $3,000 ticket and post up in the lobby of the main conference hotel taking meetings all day; the serendipity happens there too.
ideas.detail: A friend of Jean's arranges back-to-back meetings with attendees without buying a ticket. Cherie, ticketless at the most recent VidCon, sat working in the Hilton lobby without headphones, started chatting with a man four feet away, and he became a LinkedIn connection who introduced her to a useful media contact. It requires getting over the fear of being cringe or rejected.

ideas.idea: Prepare by getting the attendee list (ask organizers if needed), checking Eventbrite/Partiful guest lists for side events, and researching speakers, then reach out to targets before the conference to set up time.
ideas.detail: Jean's template: 'I saw you're going to this conference, I'd love to connect while we're both in Miami.' Looking someone up takes three seconds and can surface a career overlap or business deal. Summary: be prepared, then attend with a fun, open attitude rather than pressure to achieve.

ideas.idea: When communicating with executives above your direct boss, think 'Twitter, not Tolstoy': keep it high level and lead with the new information or value you bring so they can grok it in minimal time.
ideas.detail: Cherie learned this framework in her Stanford GSB communications class; the goal is to make a good impression without wasting a senior person's time.

ideas.idea: Practice the 15-minute, 5-minute and 2-minute versions of any update for a senior leader; deliver the two-minute version and let them ask for more or send details by email.
ideas.detail: The exercise forces you to distill the takeaways; Jean notes you often only catch an executive for a couple of minutes between meetings and they need enough to decide quickly. The same applies to written emails with sub-bullets.

ideas.idea: Don't be rigid or scripted with executives; know your material deeply enough to react to curveballs and have a real conversation, because they want to work with a person, not a robot, and can sniff out inauthenticity.
ideas.detail: Cherie says knowing the material is the deeper layer of preparedness that frees you from talking points; 'be chill, be funny, be yourself' if the environment is safe, without revealing every inner demon.

ideas.idea: A trusting relationship with your boss or VP earns you mutual benefit of the doubt, which cuts your workload roughly in half compared with the mental gymnastics of a low-trust relationship.
ideas.detail: Cherie's most fruitful relationship was with a VP at LinkedIn she worked with for years and was on texting terms with; if he snapped on a bad day she would not fall apart, and if she was off one day he trusted her. Jean has been on the other side and says the extra 'how will they take this' overthinking is ten times the work.

ideas.idea: Bringing your whole, obviously-caring self to work makes managers give you the benefit of the doubt, and likability plus relating to all kinds of people is a career superpower.
ideas.detail: Cherie says her bosses know she is a 'try hard' who cries because she cares, so they extend grace; Jean identifies likability and relating across types of people as one of Cherie's superpowers.

ideas.idea: To exit a conversation, pre-arrange for your buddy to come pull you out in 15-20 minutes, with a signal to wave them off if the conversation is good.
ideas.detail: This takes the pressure off you, like the friend rescue signal at a party but in a professional setting; the risk is the buddy forgets or is in the bathroom.

ideas.idea: Otherwise the onus is on you to speak up: at networking events you only need the thinnest excuse plus a close, such as 'I need to say goodbye to Amy before I go, let's connect on LinkedIn'.
ideas.detail: Politely pivot, thank them, and propose exchanging information to continue later. Just saying 'I'm going to get water' is not enough because they may follow you or expect you back; pair the refill with a clear goodbye.
